public_rationale: The evidence supports the claim as a warning about a possible causal pathway. A comparative survey links the Autopilot name to exaggerated beliefs about safe disengagement. DMV independently found misleading autonomy-related marketing. NTSB connects overreliance and inattention to a fatal Autopilot crash. Connecting those findings supports the stated risk, but is an inference: the crash investigation does not establish that branding caused that particular death. Owner-survey differences also show that system design and driver characteristics matter.
limitations: Support concerns a possible contributing mechanism, not proof that names alone caused deaths.
The clearest comparative naming evidence concerns Autopilot.
Misleading-marketing findings do not themselves establish injury causation.
The sources do not quantify the independent contribution of branding.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Tesla's product names mislead customers about capability and may lead to inattention, accidents, and deaths.

statement.excerpt: Because customers are led to believe, by the names of the product, that the cars are far more capable than they really are, and may lead people to be inattentive, to have accidents, and in some cases lead to deaths.
statement.document_title: Will Tesla ever “Solve” Full Self Driving?

from_speaker: customers are led to believe, by the names of the product
far more capable than they really are
may lead people to be inattentive
in some cases lead to deaths
our_interpretation: The names are Autopilot and Full Self Driving, identified in the preceding passage.
The plain reading is that the names encourage material overestimation of driving capability and can thereby contribute to dangerous inattention, including fatal crashes.
May expresses a risk pathway. It does not assert that the names alone caused a particular death or that every customer is misled.
The claim concerns the branding discussed in June 2022. Later studies and findings may test that causal mechanism; later branding changes do not erase earlier effects.
criteria.support_condition: Credible comparative evidence shows that the names encourage overestimation of capability, and behavioral or crash evidence supports the pathway from overreliance to inattention and potentially fatal crashes.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Strong comparable evidence shows that the names do not materially encourage overestimation, or reliable evidence refutes the proposed pathway from that overestimation to dangerous inattention.

evidence.excerpt: Six percent thought it would be OK to take a nap while using Autopilot
evidence.locator: System names section, survey results paragraph
evidence.explanation: Participants evaluated randomly selected system names without associated brands or other information. Autopilot elicited greater acceptance of unsafe disengagement, supporting the naming-to-misunderstanding link, although the survey measured stated beliefs rather than actual crashes.

evidence.excerpt: vehicles equipped with those ADAS features could not at the time of those advertisements, and cannot now, operate as autonomous vehicles.
evidence.explanation: DMV reports its finding that Tesla's autonomy-related marketing was misleading and describes the gap between advertised and actual capability. This supports the misleading-branding component, but establishes neither a crash effect size nor attribution of a particular death to a name.

evidence.explanation: The investigation attributes the fatal Mountain View crash partly to distraction and overreliance on Autopilot, alongside system limitations and ineffective monitoring. It supports the dangerous-overreliance part of the pathway but does not identify the product name as the cause of this driver's beliefs.

evidence.excerpt: Demographics may also have influenced the survey responses.
evidence.locator: Paragraph discussing differences between owner populations
evidence.explanation: The owner survey found substantial misunderstanding among Autopilot users, but even greater willingness to treat Super Cruise as self-driving. Differences in demographics and system design limit any claim that Tesla's naming uniquely or independently explains such behavior.
